message:
QUESTION:
Which supplier, A or B, should the firm use for component K-220, given that a delivery taking longer than 26 days causes a stockout?

DATA:
Choosing a supplier for component K-220. Safety stock covers lead times of up to 26 days. Any delivery that takes longer than 26 days causes a stockout, which halts the assembly line.

Last 12 orders from each supplier, lead time in days (order placed to goods received), in date order:
Supplier A (sea freight): 21, 23, 22, 24, 20, 22, 45, 23, 21, 22, 24, 21
Supplier B (road and rail): 18, 19, 30, 17, 29, 18, 31, 19, 28, 18, 30, 19

Notes:
- A's 45-day delivery was the order shipped in February, during the documented three-week national port strike, which delayed all sea freight that month. There has been no strike since, and none is planned.
- B had no comparable disruption. B's deliveries of 28 days or more are spread throughout the year.
- Unit price: A £4.10, B £4.05. Annual volume about 40,000 units.
- Both suppliers meet the quality specification for K-220.
- This decision applies to K-220 only. Other components are bought under separate contracts with different specifications, volumes and routes.

<analysis>
**Recommendation: Supplier A.** A delivers within the 26-day cover in normal conditions. B breaches it on roughly two orders in five, and possibly one in two. B's 5p price advantage is far too small to pay for those stoppages.

## Lead-time reliability

**Supplier A.** Eleven of A's 12 deliveries took 20–24 days, which left at least 2 days of margin inside the cover. The one exception, at 45 days, was shipped during the documented three-week national port strike, which delayed all sea freight that month. There has been no strike since and none is planned. The strike was an external event and is not evidence of how A normally performs.

**Supplier B.** B's lead times form two separate clusters, with nothing between 19 and 28 days:
- a fast cluster at 17–19 days;
- a slow cluster at 28–31 days.

Every order in the slow cluster breached the 26-day cover. That was 5 of 12 orders, or about two in five. From order 3 onward, every other order was slow (orders 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11). Orders 1 and 2 were both fast. That regularity points to a recurring cause, such as alternating routes, carriers or depots, rather than random delay. Twelve orders cannot prove this, but nothing in the data suggests it will stop. If the alternation continues, B's future breach rate would be closer to **one in two** than two in five.

## Why the simpler measures point the wrong way

| | Mean (days) | Worst case (days) | Range (days) | Deliveries over 26 days |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A, all 12 orders | 24.0 | 45 | 20–45 | 1 (strike) |
| A, excluding strike order | 22.1 | 24 | 20–24 | 0 of 11 |
| B | 23.0 | 31 | 17–31 | 5 of 12 |

Measured over all 12 orders, B appears better on mean, worst case and range. None of these measures reflects what actually stops the line:
- **Mean.** B's fast deliveries offset its slow ones in the average, but the line stops on every slow delivery.
- **Worst case and range.** A looks worse only because of the single strike-affected order. Without that order, A's worst case is 24 days.

The measure that matters is the number of deliveries over 26 days, and on that measure A is clearly better.

## Is the difference just chance?

Twelve orders per supplier is a small sample. Even so, A had 0 breaches in 11 normal orders, compared with 5 in 12 for B. If both suppliers really had the same breach rate, a split this uneven would be unlikely (Fisher's exact test, one-sided, p ≈ 0.02).

This result depends on excluding the strike order. If that order is counted as a breach (1 in 12 against 5 in 12), p ≈ 0.08, which is not significant at the 5% level. Excluding it is justified because the notes document the strike as a one-off external event that affected all sea freight. The gap between the suppliers remains large under either treatment, but the formal significance test relies on treating the strike as exceptional.

## Price

B is 5p per unit cheaper (£4.05 against £4.10, about 1.2%). At roughly 40,000 units a year, that saves about £2,000 annually.

For B to come out ahead, that £2,000 must be greater than the cost of B's extra stoppages. Using B's record of about 5 stoppages per 12 orders:

| Orders per year | Expected B stoppages per year | B wins only if each stoppage costs less than |
|---|---|---|
| 12 (monthly) | about 5 | about £400 |
| 52 (weekly)* | about 22 | about £90 |

Order frequency is not given, so these figures are illustrative. If B's alternation continues and its breach rate approaches one in two, the thresholds fall further. Stopping an assembly line almost certainly costs more than either figure.

\*The weekly row follows the brief's rule that any delivery over 26 days causes a stockout. With weekly ordering, several orders would be in transit at once, and a late delivery might sometimes be covered by a later order arriving early. That would lower B's actual stoppage count, but it would need stoppage costs well under £100 to change the conclusion.

## Quality

Both suppliers meet the K-220 specification, so quality does not separate them.

## Risks and caveats

- **Strike exposure.** A relies on sea freight and remains exposed to port disruption. No strike has occurred since February and none is planned, but a future one cannot be ruled out. *Mitigation:* when port disruption is signalled, first raise safety stock temporarily to cover the expected delay. Moving orders to B is a secondary option, because B's own breach rate is about 40–50% unless safety stock is also raised.
- **Small sample.** Twelve orders per supplier is limited evidence, and the formal significance depends on how the strike order is treated (see above). Quarterly monitoring will show whether the difference holds.
- **B could improve.** If B finds and fixes the cause of its 28–31-day deliveries, it could become competitive. The other way to make B workable is to raise safety stock to cover about 32 days, but holding more inventory has its own cost. Both options are worth revisiting at the next review.

## Scope

This decision covers K-220 only. Other components are bought under separate contracts with different specifications, volumes and routes. This data says nothing about which supplier suits those components, so it should not be used to consolidate them with either supplier.

## Actions

1. Award the K-220 contract to **Supplier A**.
2. Review lead-time performance quarterly, tracking the **number of deliveries over 26 days** rather than the average.
3. Keep **Supplier B** as a qualified back-up, and pair any switch to B with a temporary increase in safety stock.
4. Ask B why, from order 3 onward, every other delivery has been slow, and whether this reflects alternating routes, carriers or depots. Reconsider B if it resolves the cause.

---

*Change notes:*
- *An earlier version gave B's mean as 22.0 days. The correct figure is 23.0 days (276 ÷ 12). That version also recommended B on the basis of mean lead time, worst case and range, and proposed consolidating other components with B. Both have been withdrawn for the reasons above.*
- *This revision:*
  - *puts the recommendation first;*
  - *corrects the description of B's alternation (it starts at order 3, not order 1);*
  - *discloses that the significance test is sensitive to the strike order (p ≈ 0.02 excluding it, ≈ 0.08 including it);*
  - *adds a comparison table of the simple measures;*
  - *footnotes the overlapping-orders assumption behind the weekly break-even figure;*
  - *makes a temporary safety-stock increase the main strike mitigation.*
</analysis>

Produce the final version of this analysis.
